claim: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) has been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as an evidence-based treatment for patients with migraine, major depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and smoking addiction.
source: Further, one particular form of neuromodulation, transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), has been approved by regulatory bodies in multiple countries, including the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and is used as an evidence-based treatment for patients with migraine, major depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and smoking addiction (Hallett, 2007; Walsh and Cowey, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hallett, 2007 and Walsh and Cowey, 2000, which provide external scholarly support for the FDA approval and clinical applications of TMS.

claim: TMS and other neuromodulatory devices have been highlighted as potential treatments for psychiatric, neurological, and neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: Moreover, TMS and other neuromodulatory devices, such as transcranial-focused ultrasound and electrical stimulation (tES), have been highlighted as a potential treatment for psychiatric, neurological, and neurodevelopmental disorders (Grover et al., 2021; Khedr et al., 2005; McGough et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Grover et al., 2021; Khedr et al., 2005; and McGough et al., 2019, which provide scholarly references for the potential therapeutic applications.

claim: TMS and tES have been used to enhance various mental processes, including attention, memory, language, mathematics, and intelligence in healthy populations.
source: and they have also been used to enhance various mental processes, including attention, memory, language, mathematics, and intelligence in healthy populations (Santarnecchi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Santarnecchi et al., 2015, which provides scholarly evidence for cognitive enhancement applications in healthy individuals.

claim: Contradictory findings have emerged across different studies regarding the beneficial effects of both TMS and tES.
source: Despite some encouraging results on the beneficial effects of both TMS and tES, contradictory findings have emerged across different studies (Horvath et al., 2015; Medina and Cason, 2017; Parkin et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018; Westwood et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Horvath et al., 2015; Medina and Cason, 2017; Parkin et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018; Westwood et al., 2017) that document inconsistent research findings.

claim: Participants who take part in TMS and tES studies consistently report various perceptual sensations, such as audible clicks, visual disturbances, and cutaneous sensations.
source: Participants who take part in TMS and tES studies consistently report various perceptual sensations, such as audible clicks, visual disturbances, and cutaneous sensations (Davis et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Davis et al., 2013, which provides scholarly evidence for the perceptual sensations experienced during neurostimulation.

claim: 84% of 173 tDCS studies used similar sham approaches to an early method by Gandiga et al., 2006.
source: A review by Fonteneau et al., 2019 shows that 84% of 173 studies used similar sham approaches to an early method by Gandiga et al., 2006.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fonteneau et al., 2019 and Gandiga et al., 2006, which provide scholarly evidence for the prevalence of specific sham protocols in tDCS research.

claim: The initial tDCS sham protocol had a 10 s ramp-up followed by 30 s of active stimulation at 1 mA before cessation, differently from active stimulation that typically lasts up to 20 min.
source: This initial protocol had a 10 s ramp-up followed by 30 s of active stimulation at 1 mA before cessation, differently from active stimulation that typically lasts up to 20 min.
evidence: The claim is based on a description of established sham protocols in the field, drawing from scientific knowledge about tDCS methodology.

claim: Sham treatments aim to simulate the perceptual sensations associated with active stimulation without substantially affecting cortical excitability.
source: Overall, these types of sham stimulation aim to simulate the perceptual sensations associated with active stimulation without substantially affecting cortical excitability (Fritsch et al., 2010; Nitsche and Paulus, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fritsch et al., 2010 and Nitsche and Paulus, 2000, which provide scholarly evidence for the mechanism and purpose of sham stimulation.

claim: In Study 1, 121 patients aged 18–85 with treatment-resistant depression were randomised to receive either bilateral rTMS, unilateral left-rTMS, or sham rTMS for 3 or 6 weeks.
source: In study 1 (Blumberger et al., 2016), patients aged 18–85 with treatment-resistant depression (N = 121) were randomised to receive either bilateral rTMS, unilateral left-rTMS, or sham rTMS for 3 or 6 weeks (objective treatment).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design and participant characteristics from Study 1, which is based on data from Blumberger et al., 2016.

claim: In Study 1, the two-way interaction between subjective treatment and time led to a significantly higher model fit (BIC = 2027.48, AIC = 1985.62, p<0.001).
source: Our results showed that the two-way interaction between subjective treatment and time led to a significantly higher model fit (Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) = 2027.48, Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) = 1985.62, p<0.001; see Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from the analysis of Study 1 data, including specific model fit metrics and p-values.

claim: In Study 1, participants who thought they received active stimulation showed a steeper decrease in depression over time than participants who thought they received sham.
source: As shown in Figure 1, participants who thought they received active stimulation showed a steeper decrease in depression over time than participants who thought they received sham.
evidence: The claim is supported by both the text description and Figure 1, which shows the depression scores over time for different subjective treatment groups.

claim: In Study 1, depression scores were lower for participants who thought they were receiving active compared to sham stimulation at week 6 (b = -6.72, t(321) = -6.84, p< 0.001).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from contrast analysis of Study 1 data, including regression coefficients, t-statistics, and p-values.

claim: In Study 1, the inclusion of neither objective treatment nor the objective treatment by time interaction led to a better model fit when subjective treatment was already in the model.
source: Our results showed that the inclusion of neither objective treatment nor the objective treatment by time interaction led to a better model fit (Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: The claim presents results from model comparison analysis of Study 1 data, indicating that objective treatment did not improve model fit beyond subjective treatment.

claim: In Study 1, the model with subjective treatment as a main effect led to a significantly better fit for HAMD-17 response rate (deviance = 15.08, p = 0.0001).
source: Our results showed that the model with subjective treatment as a main effect led to a significantly better fit (deviance = 15.08, p = 0.0001; see Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from model comparison analysis of Study 1 response rate data, including deviance and p-values.

claim: In Study 1, response rates on HAMD-17 were higher for participants who reported thinking they received the active compared to the sham treatment (log(OR) = 2.61, z = 3.21, SE = 0.81, p = 0.001).
source: As shown in Figure 2, response rates were higher for participants who reported thinking they received the active compared to the sham treatment (log(OR) = 2.61, z = 3.21, SE = 0.81, p = 0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by both the text description and Figure 2, which shows response rates by subjective treatment, along with statistical parameters.

claim: In Study 1, objective treatment did not explain changes in patients' depression when subjective beliefs were already accounted for in the model (deviance = 1.40, p = 0.496).
source: On the contrary, when we examined whether the addition of objective treatment to a model already including subjective treatment led to a better fit, this was not the case (deviance = 1.40, p = 0.496; see Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from model comparison analysis showing that objective treatment did not improve model fit when subjective treatment was already included.

claim: In Study 1, the same pattern of results for subjective treatment was replicated for response rates calculated based on the Beck Depression Inventory II (BDI-II), where subjective treatment as a main effect led to a significantly better model fit (deviance = 10.81, p = 0.001).
source: The same pattern of results was replicated for response rates calculated based on another depression scale, the Beck Depression Inventory II (BDI-II), where subjective treatment as a main effect led to a significantly better model fit (deviance = 10.81, p = 0.001; see Figure 2—source data 3)
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from model comparison analysis of BDI-II response rate data, showing replication of the subjective treatment effect.

claim: In Study 1, participants who reported the active subjective treatment showed higher BDI-II response rates (log(OR) = 1.85, z = 3.06, SE = 0.60, p = 0.002).
source: and participants who reported the active subjective treatment showed higher response rates (log(OR) = 1.85, z = 3.06, SE = 0.60, p = 0.002).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from analysis of BDI-II response rates by subjective treatment.

claim: In Study 1, objective treatment did not provide a better model fit than subjective treatment for BDI-II response rates (deviance = 0.27, p = 0.873).
source: In contrast, objective treatment did not provide a better model fit than subjective treatment (deviance = 0.27, p = 0.873; see Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from model comparison analysis showing that objective treatment did not improve model fit for BDI-II response rates.

claim: In Study 1, remitters were defined by a HAMD-17 score ≤7 at the end of weeks 3 and 6.
source: Additionally, in the study, participants were classified as either remitters or non-remitters based on blinded clinical ratings at the end of weeks 3 and 6, defined by a HAMD-17 score ≤7.
evidence: The claim describes the operational definition of remission used in Study 1, which is a methodological detail from the original study.

claim: In Study 1, for objective treatment, the survival curves did not significantly differ between the active and sham condition (Gehan–Breslow–Wilcoxon test(1) = 3.72, p = 0.053).
source: We found that, for objective treatment, the survival curves did not significantly differ between the active and sham condition (Gehan–Breslow–Wilcoxon test(1) = 3.72, p = 0.053)
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from survival analysis of remission rates by objective treatment.

claim: In Study 1, for subjective treatment, a significant difference in survival curves emerged (Gehan–Breslow–Wilcoxon test(1) = 18.16, p< 0.001).
source: On the contrary, for subjective treatment, a significant difference emerged (Gehan–Breslow–Wilcoxon test(1) = 18.16, p< 0.001).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from survival analysis of remission rates by subjective treatment.

claim: In Study 1, patients who reported they believed receiving active stimulation showed higher remission rates than patients who believed they received sham (Gehan–Breslow–Wilcoxon test(1) = 5.12, p = 0.020).
source: Specifically, patients who reported they believed receiving active stimulation showed higher remission rates than patients who believed they received sham (Gehan–Breslow–Wilcoxon test(1) = 5.12, p = 0.020).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from survival analysis comparing remission rates between subjective treatment groups.

claim: In Study 2, 52 participants aged 60-85 diagnosed with late-life depression were randomised to active or sham high-dose deep rTMS.
source: In study 2 (Kaster et al., 2018), 52 participants aged 60-85 diagnosed with late-life depression were randomised to active or sham high-dose deep rTMS.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design and participant characteristics from Study 2, which is based on data from Kaster et al., 2018.

claim: Deep rTMS with the H1 coil has been designed to stimulate deeper and larger areas of the cortex (primarily the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex - DLPFC - and portions of the right DLPFC).
source: Compared to standard rTMS, deep rTMS with the H1 coil has been designed to stimulate deeper and larger areas of the cortex (primarily the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex - DLPFC - and portions of the right DLPFC).
evidence: The claim describes the technical characteristics of deep rTMS with the H1 coil, which is established knowledge about this neurostimulation technique.

claim: In Study 2, participants were asked to report whether they thought they received the active or sham treatment after the first week of treatment rather than at the end.
source: Notably, in contrast to the other studies, participants were asked to report whether they thought they received the active or sham treatment after the first week of treatment rather than at the end (i.e., fourth week).
evidence: The claim describes a methodological detail of Study 2 regarding the timing of subjective treatment assessment.

claim: In Study 2, the three-way interaction model (subjective treatment by objective treatment by time) led to a significantly better fit (AIC = 1601.91, BIC = 1668.75, p = 0.011).
source: Our results showed that the three-way interaction model led to a significantly better fit (AIC = 1601.91, BIC = 1668.75, p = 0.011; see Figure 3—source data 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from model comparison analysis of Study 2 data, including model fit metrics and p-values.

claim: In Study 2, there was a steeper decrease in depression from baseline to week 3 (b = 8.79, t(102.57) = 2.01, SE = 4.37, p = 0.047) for active objective treatment and active subjective treatment compared to sham treatment.
source: We found a steeper decrease in depression from baseline to week 3 (b = 8.79, t(102.57) = 2.01, SE = 4.37, p = 0.047)
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from contrast analysis of Study 2 data examining the three-way interaction effect.

claim: In Study 2, there was a steeper decrease in depression from baseline to week 4 (b = 9.19, t(103.80) = 2.10, SE = 4.39, p = 0.039) for active objective treatment and active subjective treatment compared to sham treatment.
source: and from baseline to week 4 (b = 9.19, t(103.80) = 2.10, SE = 4.39, p = 0.039).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from contrast analysis of Study 2 data examining the three-way interaction effect.

claim: In Study 2, the objective and subjective treatment differed in the linear contrast of time (b = 28.03, t(182.30) = 3.13, p = 0.002).
source: The analysis showed that the objective and subjective treatment differed in the linear contrast of time (b = 28.03, t(182.30) = 3.13, p = 0.002).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from polynomial contrast analysis of Study 2 data examining the three-way interaction.

claim: In Study 2, the contrast showed a negative slope throughout the weeks that were significantly different between the objective treatment levels in the subjective sham treatment (b = -19.63, t(181.05) = -2.77, p = 0.001), but not for the subjective active treatment (b = 8.40, t(184.33) = 1.52, p = 0.128).
source: The contrast showed a negative slope throughout the weeks that were significantly different between the objective treatment levels in the subjective sham treatment (b = -19.63, t(181.05) = -2.77, p = 0.001), but not for the subjective active treatment (b = 8.40, t(184.33) = 1.52, p = 0.128).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from contrast analysis examining the differential effects of objective treatment within subjective treatment groups.

claim: In Study 2, the steepest change in depression occurred among those who received the active treatment but believed they received the sham treatment (compared to those who believed they received the active treatment).
source: Thus, the results show that the steepest change in depression occurred among those who received the active treatment but believed they received the sham treatment (compared to those who believed they received the active treatment).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the statistical results from Study 2, summarizing the pattern of depression changes across treatment groups.

claim: In Study 2, the interaction of subjective treatment by objective treatment was significantly better at predicting remission rates (deviance = 4.47, p = 0.035).
source: In line with our previous results, we found that the interaction of subjective treatment by objective treatment was significantly better at predicting remission rates (deviance = 4.47, p = 0.035; see Figure 4—source data 1 and 2)
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from model comparison analysis of Study 2 remission rate data.

claim: In Study 2, the interaction of subjective treatment by objective treatment was significantly better at predicting response rates (deviance = 8.17, p=0.004).
source: and response rates (deviance = 8.17, p=0.004; see Figure 4—source data 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from model comparison analysis of Study 2 response rate data.

claim: In Study 2, for remission rates, there was a significant two-way interaction between objective treatment and subjective treatment (log(OR) = 0.81, z = 1.99, SE = 0.41, p = 0.047).
source: For remission rates, we found a significant two-way interaction between objective treatment and subjective treatment (log(OR) = 0.81, z = 1.99, SE = 0.41, p = 0.047, Figure 4).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from analysis of remission rates, supported by both text and Figure 4.

claim: In Study 2, for remission rates, the effect did not differ significantly between active and sham rTMS as the objective treatment when participants thought they received the active stimulation (b = -1.01, z = -0.82, SE = 1.23, p = 0.410).
source: While the effect did not differ significantly between active and sham rTMS as the objective treatment when participants thought they received the active stimulation (b = -1.01, z = -0.82, SE = 1.23, p = 0.410)
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from contrast analysis of remission rates within the subjective active treatment group.

claim: In Study 2, for remission rates, higher remission rates were found when patients thought they received sham (b = 2.69, SE = 1.29, z = 2.08, p = 0.038).
source: higher remission rates were found when patients thought they received sham (b = 2.69, SE = 1.29, z = 2.08, p = 0.038).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from contrast analysis of remission rates within the subjective sham treatment group.

claim: In Study 2, for response rates, there was a significant two-way interaction (log(OR) = 1.02, z = 2.58, SE = 0.4, p = 0.010).
source: These results were replicated when we considered response rates as the outcome (Figures 4) for which we found a significant two-way interaction (log(OR) = 1.02, z = 2.58, SE = 0.4, p = 0.010).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from analysis of response rates, supported by both text and Figure 4.

claim: In Study 2, for response rates, for participants who thought they received the active stimulation, remission did not differ significantly between active and sham rTMS as the objective treatment (b = -1.7, z = -1.44, SE = 1.18, p = 0.150).
source: Again, for participants who thought they received the active stimulation, remission did not differ significantly between active and sham rTMS as the objective treatment (b = -1.7, z = -1.44, SE = 1.18, p = 0.150).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from contrast analysis of response rates within the subjective active treatment group.

claim: In Study 2, for response rates, when participants thought they received sham stimulation, they showed higher response rates in the active compared to sham rTMS as the objective treatment (b = 2.38, SE = 1.05, z = 2.26, p = 0.020).
source: On the contrary, when participants thought they received sham stimulation, they showed higher response rates in the active compared to sham rTMS as the objective treatment (b = 2.38, SE = 1.05, z = 2.26, p = 0.020).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from contrast analysis of response rates within the subjective sham treatment group.

claim: In Study 3, researchers examined the effect of home-based tDCS treatment used for 4 weeks on a clinical group of adults diagnosed with ADHD (N = 64).
source: In study 3, the researchers examined the effect of home-based tDCS treatment used for 4 weeks on a clinical group of adults diagnosed with ADHD (Leffa et al., 2022; N = 64).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design and participant characteristics from Study 3, which is based on data from Leffa et al., 2022.

claim: In Study 3, the primary outcome measure was symptoms of inattention taken from a clinician-administered questionnaire (Adult ADHD Self-report Scale; CASRS-I).
source: The primary outcome measure was symptoms of inattention taken from a clinician-administered questionnaire (Adult ADHD Self-report Scale; CASRS-I).
evidence: The claim describes the primary outcome measure used in Study 3, which is a methodological detail from the study.

claim: In Study 3, data on participants' beliefs reflecting subjective treatment was collected at the end of the experiment.
source: Data on participants' beliefs reflecting subjective treatment was collected at the end of the experiment.
evidence: The claim describes a methodological detail of Study 3 regarding the timing of subjective treatment assessment.

claim: In Study 3, including subjective treatment led to a better model fit (AIC = 593.81, BIC = 609.79, p< 0.001).
source: In line with the studies above, we first investigated the addition of subjective treatment to a model accounting for objective treatment between the baseline and the last assessments. Including subjective treatment led to a better model fit (AIC = 593.81, BIC = 609.79, p< 0.001; see Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from model comparison analysis of Study 3 data, including model fit metrics and p-values.

claim: In Study 3, inattention scores for participants who believed they were getting the active treatment were significantly lower compared to those who believed they belonged to the sham group (b = −3.33, t(100) = -3.35, SE = 0.99, p = 0.001).
source: Subsequent contrast analysis revealed that inattention scores for participants who believed they were getting the active treatment were significantly lower compared to those who believed they belonged to the sham group (b = −3.33, t(100) = -3.35, SE = 0.99, p = 0.001, see Figure 5).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from contrast analysis of Study 3 data, supported by both text and Figure 5.

claim: In Study 3, the addition of the objective treatment was significant (AIC = 593.81, BIC = 609.79, p< 0.001) when added to a model already including subjective treatment.
source: Differently from studies 1 and 2, where this addition was not found significant, here, the addition of the objective treatment was significant (AIC = 593.81, BIC = 609.79, p< 0.001; see Figure 5—source data 3).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from model comparison analysis showing that objective treatment improved model fit even when subjective treatment was already included.

claim: In Study 3, the contrast showed lower inattention symptoms in the objective active treatment group (b = -4.17, t(100) = −4.21, SE = 0.99, p< 0.001).
source: As expected, the contrast showed lower inattention symptoms in the objective active treatment group (b = -4.17, t(100) = −4.21, SE = 0.99, p< 0.001).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from contrast analysis of Study 3 data examining the effect of objective treatment.

claim: In Study 3, subjective treatment did not fully overrule the contribution of objective treatment to research outcomes.
source: Thus, subjective treatment did not fully overrule the contribution of objective treatment to research outcomes.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the statistical results from Study 3, where both subjective and objective treatment contributed to the model.

claim: In Study 4, researchers examined the effects of different doses (current intensity) of tDCS on mind-wandering in healthy participants (N = 150).
source: In study 4, we extended our results beyond clinical populations by examining the effects of different doses (current intensity) of tDCS on mind-wandering in healthy participants (N = 150; Filmer et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design and participant characteristics from Study 4, which is based on data from Filmer et al., 2019.

claim: In Study 4, participants were asked about subjective beliefs at the end of the experiment.
source: Similar to studies 1 and 3, participants were asked about subjective beliefs at the end of the experiment.
evidence: The claim describes a methodological detail of Study 4 regarding the timing of subjective treatment assessment.

claim: In Study 4, subjective treatment contributed to a significantly better model fit (AIC = 284.72, BIC = 305.80, p = 0.045).
source: In line with studies 1 and 3, subjective treatment contributed to a significantly better model fit. Specifically, participants' beliefs explained variability in mind wandering when subjective treatment was included as a main effect on top of objective treatment (AIC = 284.72, BIC = 305.80, p = 0.045; see Figure 6—source data 2).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from model comparison analysis of Study 4 data, including model fit metrics and p-values.

claim: In Study 4, participants who believed they received active treatment showed higher mind-wandering levels than those who reported they believed to receive sham treatment (b = −0.11, SE = 0.05, t(144) = -2.01, p = 0.046).
source: Furthermore, as shown in Figure 6, participants who believed they received active treatment showed higher mind-wandering levels than those who reported they believed to receive sham treatment (b = −0.11, SE = 0.05, t(144) = -2.01, p = 0.046).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from analysis of Study 4 data, supported by both text and Figure 6.

claim: In Study 4, subjective dosage contributed to a better model fit including objective treatment (AIC = 282.90, BIC = 310, p = 0.025).
source: The experimental design in this study allowed us also to expand our previous findings by examining the contribution of subjective dosage to a model including objective treatment (AIC = 282.90, BIC = 310, p = 0.025; Figure 6—source data 4).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from model comparison analysis examining the contribution of subjective dosage in Study 4.

claim: In Study 4, mind wandering increased for people reporting weak (b = −0.31, SE = 0.14, t(142) = -2.23, p = 0.03), moderate (b = −0.27, SE = 0.12, t(142) = -2.24, p = 0.027) and strong (b = 0.47, SE = 0.19, t(142) = 2.41, p = 0.017) subjective dosage compared to none.
source: In this regard, we found that mind wandering increased for people reporting weak (b = −0.31, SE = 0.14, t(142) = -2.23, p = 0.03), moderate (b = −0.27, SE = 0.12, t(142) = -2.24, p = 0.027) and strong (b = 0.47, SE = 0.19, t(142) = 2.41, p = 0.017) subjective dosage compared to none.
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from contrast analysis examining the effect of subjective dosage on mind wandering.

claim: In Study 4, mind wandering increased proportionally as the subjective dosage increased (from none to strong).
source: These results indicate that mind wandering increased proportionally as the subjective dosage increased (from none to strong).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the statistical results from Study 4, summarizing the dose-response relationship for subjective dosage.

claim: In Study 4, participants' objective treatment did not lead to a better model fit when added to a model including subjective treatment (AIC = 284.72, BIC = 305.8, p = 0.093).
source: Conversely, our results showed that participants' objective treatment did not lead to a better model fit neither when added to a model including subjective treatment (AIC = 284.72, BIC = 305.8, p = 0.093; see Figure 6—source data 3)
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from model comparison analysis showing that objective treatment did not improve model fit when subjective treatment was already included.

claim: In Study 4, participants' objective treatment did not lead to a better model fit when added to a model including subjective dosage (AIC = 282.9, BIC = 310.0, p = 0.106).
source: nor when added to a model including subjective dosage (AIC = 282.9, BIC = 310.0, p = 0.106; see Figure 6—source data 5).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from model comparison analysis showing that objective treatment did not improve model fit when subjective dosage was already included.

claim: Participants' subjective beliefs about receiving the active vs control (sham) treatment can explain variability in the primary outcome and, in some cases, fit the observed data better than the actual treatment participants received during the experiment.
source: We demonstrate that participants' subjective beliefs about receiving the active vs control (sham) treatment are an important factor that can explain variability in the primary outcome and, in some cases, fit the observed data better than the actual treatment participants received during the experiment.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the statistical analyses across all four studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: In studies 1 and 4, the fact that participants thought to be in the active or control condition explained variability in clinical and cognitive scores to a more considerable extent than the objective treatment alone.
source: Specifically, in studies 1 and 4, the fact that participants thought to be in the active or control condition explained variability in clinical and cognitive scores to a more considerable extent than the objective treatment alone.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the findings from studies 1 and 4, based on the statistical analyses presented for those studies.

claim: In study 2, the greatest improvement in depressive symptoms was observed in the group that received the active objective treatment but believed they received sham.
source: Specifically, in study 2 we observed an interaction effect, whereby the greatest improvement in depressive symptoms was observed in the group that received the active objective treatment but believed they received sham.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the findings from study 2, based on the statistical analyses showing the three-way interaction effect.

claim: In study 3, the inclusion of both subjective and objective treatment as main effects explained variability in symptoms of inattention.
source: Differently, in study 3, the inclusion of both subjective and objective treatment as main effects explained variability in symptoms of inattention.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the findings from study 3, based on the statistical analyses showing that both subjective and objective treatment contributed to the model.

claim: The variability in the observed results could be explained by factors such as participants' personality, disorder type and severity, prior treatments, knowledge base, experimental procedures, and beliefs of the research team.
source: The variability in the observed results could be explained by factors such as participants' personality, disorder type and severity, prior treatments, knowledge base, experimental procedures, and beliefs of the research team, all of which could be interesting avenues for future studies to explore.
evidence: The claim is a speculative statement about potential factors that could explain the variability in results across studies.

claim: In study 2, subjective beliefs about treatment allocation were documented before the emergence of changes in any clinical outcome.
source: Given that subjective beliefs about treatment allocation were documented before the emergence of changes in any clinical outcome, it is more plausible that participants' beliefs would have affected experimental outcomes rather than vice versa.
evidence: The claim describes a methodological feature of study 2 and draws an inference about the causal direction of the relationship between beliefs and outcomes.

claim: Placebo effects have been shown to impact not only behaviour but also brain activity.
source: We argue that the answer to this question is likely to be positive since placebo effects have been shown to impact not only behaviour but also brain activity (Fonteneau et al., 2019; Hashmi, 2018; Oken et al., 2008; Schmidt et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fonteneau et al., 2019; Hashmi, 2018; Oken et al., 2008; and Schmidt et al., 2014, which provide scholarly evidence for placebo effects on brain activity.

claim: In most RCTs investigating the effect of different treatments on clinical and subclinical groups, the measurement of symptomatology is mostly based on self-reported outcomes, such as questionnaires.
source: Noteworthy, in most RCTs investigating the effect of different treatments on clinical and subclinical groups (e.g. depression, chronic pain, eating disorders, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder), some of which have also been approved by the FDA, the measurement of symptomatology is mostly based on self-reported outcomes, such as questionnaires.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about the methodology commonly used in clinical trials.

claim: Expectations regarding the effectiveness of cognitive training (i.e. whether it will increase or decrease performance) can significantly modulate its effect.
source: Indeed, as recently shown by Parong et al., 2022, expectations regarding the effectiveness of cognitive training (i.e. whether it will increase or decrease performance) can significantly modulate its effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Parong et al., 2022, which provides scholarly evidence for the role of expectations in cognitive training outcomes.

claim: In Study 1 (Blumberger et al., 2016), all participants received treatment five times per week over 3 weeks for 15 treatments, only delivered on weekdays.
